meta.description: Elie Wiesel really said it in 1986 — but the line was published 65 years earlier by psychoanalyst Wilhelm Stekel in 1921. The full provenance.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The opposite of love is not hate, it's indifference'?
meta.ogDescription: Wiesel said it in 1986, but didn't coin it — the exact formulation is Wilhelm Stekel's, published in 1921.

answer.label: Not original to Elie Wiesel — the formulation is Wilhelm Stekel’s (1921)
answer.sourceLine: Elie Wiesel really did say this exact line — in a 1986 U.S. News & World Report interview (“The opposite of love is not hate, it’s indifference…”) — so it is a genuine Wiesel quotation. But he did not coin it: Quote Investigator traces the same formulation to the Austrian psychoanalyst Wilhelm Stekel, who wrote “The opposite of love is not hate, but indifference” in a book published in 1921 — seven years before Wiesel was even born. The misattribution is one of origin, not fabrication.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: The Beloved Ego: Foundations of the New Study of the Psyche

source.excerpt: Indifference, to me, is the epitome of evil. The opposite of love is not hate, it’s indifference. The opposite of art is not ugliness, it’s indifference. The opposite of faith is not heresy, it’s indifference. And the opposite of life is not death, it’s indifference.
trail: Quote Investigator finds the earliest close match in Wilhelm Stekel’s The Beloved Ego (translated by Rosalie Gabler, 1921): “The opposite of love is not hate, but indifference.”
Wiesel did use the exact line — in a 1986 U.S. News & World Report interview — but that was 65 years after Stekel and is not originary.
Goodreads credits the line to Stekel and tags it “misattributed-elie-wiesel.”
Cousin phrasings run through John le Carré (1968, “apathy”) and Rollo May (1969), per QI.
source.excerptNote: Elie Wiesel, interview in U.S. News & World Report, 1986. Wiesel’s wording is genuine — but the near-identical formulation had already appeared in Wilhelm Stekel’s 1921 The Beloved Ego: “The opposite of love is not hate, but indifference; the opposite of feeling can only be the absence of feeling.”

source.rightsNote: The exact wording as quoted — “it’s indifference” — is Elie Wiesel’s 1986 phrasing, which is in copyright. The near-identical originating formulation (“but indifference”) appeared in Rosalie Gabler’s 1921 translation of Stekel, published before 1931 and therefore itself in the public domain; but the specific string people quote traces to Wiesel’s modern statement, so the conservative rights status is in-copyright.

author.name: Wilhelm Stekel
author.heading: Who actually wrote it
author.bio: Wilhelm Stekel was an Austrian physician and one of Sigmund Freud’s earliest followers, later an independent psychoanalyst known for his work on the psychology of love, sexuality, and the emotions. In his 1921 book The Beloved Ego (and its German counterpart the same year) he set down the antithesis that would later travel the world under other names: that the true opposite of love is not hatred but indifference — the absence of feeling.

misattribution.heading: How Wiesel got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is an unusual case: the person it’s credited to really did say it. What’s wrong is the belief that he originated it.

items.why: Wiesel used the exact line in a 1986 U.S. News & World Report interview, but the formulation predates him by 65 years: Wilhelm Stekel published it in his 1921 book The Beloved Ego, per Quote Investigator. Wiesel was born in 1928 — after the line was already in print.

It’s often assumed the “life” clause — “the opposite of life is not death, it’s indifference” — is a later viral add-on, but it isn’t: Wiesel’s documented 1986 statement already ran to four parallel clauses (love, art, faith, life), opening with “Indifference, to me, is the epitome of evil,” per Quote Investigator. The widely shared four-part version (see Goodreads) is the real 1986 wording, not an over-expansion.

misattribution.truthLine: Wiesel genuinely said it in 1986 — but the thought was Wilhelm Stekel’s in 1921, with cousin phrasings from John le Carré (1968) and Rollo May (1969), all charted by Quote Investigator.

context.heading: Why it stuck to Wiesel
lead: The line resonates under Elie Wiesel’s name for a reason: as a survivor of Auschwitz and Buchenwald and a Nobel Peace Prize laureate, Wiesel spent his life warning that indifference — not active hatred alone — is what lets atrocity happen. When he repeated the aphorism in 1986, it landed with the moral authority of lived witness, and it fused to him.

But an idea can be spoken powerfully without being invented by the speaker. The near-identical sentence had already been printed in 1921 by the psychoanalyst Wilhelm Stekel, and related versions circulated for decades before Wiesel ever used it.
context.pull: Wiesel gave the line its moral weight — but not its words.
